opus-5.5.text:
I think we're going to see progress much faster than most people expect. SWE-bench is a good benchmark because it's grounded in real GitHub issues from real repositories, so you can't just pattern-match your way through it. You actually have to understand a codebase, figure out what's wrong, write a fix, and make sure it passes the tests. That's very close to what a software engineer does day to day.

Getting to 50% feels quite near to me. A lot of the gains come not just from better base models but from better scaffolding: letting the agent explore the repository, run code, look at test failures, and iterate. Once you give a model the ability to try things, observe the outcome, and correct itself, performance jumps significantly. That's the same lesson we learned in reinforcement learning with systems like AlphaGo and AlphaZero. Search and feedback loops are incredibly powerful when you have a reliable signal, and in coding the tests give you that signal.

Going from 50% to 90% is a different story. The remaining problems tend to be the hard ones: issues that are underspecified, that require deep understanding of the design intent of a large codebase, or where the tests themselves are ambiguous. Some of the tasks in the benchmark might be borderline unsolvable without extra context a human maintainer would have. So the last stretch will be slower, and it will probably require real advances in reasoning and planning over long horizons, not just more compute at inference time.

Still, if you'd asked me a few years ago whether we'd even be having this conversation, I'd have been skeptical. My honest view is that 50% is a matter of a year or so, and 90% is a few years out. The bottleneck will be less about raw capability and more about reliability: making sure the agent knows when it's confident, when it's stuck, and when it should ask for help. That's what will make these systems truly useful to engineers, more than any single benchmark number.

r001.rationale: “50% is a matter of a year or so” places the estimate within the one-to-three-year window.

r002.rationale: “90% is a few years out” gives no clear estimate that falls within the specified three-to-five-year window.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a good question, and I want to be careful with it, because I think the two thresholds are actually very different kinds of questions.

Fifty percent on SWE-bench, honestly, I think we're basically already there, depending on which version you look at. On Verified, the top systems crossed that a while ago. So the interesting question isn't whether we get to fifty, it's what fifty actually told us. And what it told us is that the agent loop works. You give a model the ability to read the repo, run tests, iterate on its own output, and you get a very large jump over a single forward pass. That was the lesson of the first phase, and it was mostly an infrastructure lesson, not a capability lesson.

Ninety percent is where I get more cautious. The remaining tail of that benchmark isn't uniformly hard in one direction. Some of the failures are tasks where the model genuinely can't reason through the codebase. But a lot of them are things like underspecified issues, where the "correct" patch is really the one a specific maintainer happened to write, and there are other valid solutions that fail the hidden tests. Or the environment doesn't quite reproduce. So some fraction of the gap to ninety is not about intelligence at all, it's about the benchmark having noise in it. That's why people built the Verified subset in the first place.

So if you ask me for a timeline, I'd split it. For the capability part, the part where the model actually understands a large unfamiliar codebase and makes a correct multi-file change, I think the trend lines from the last two years are pretty steep, and I don't see a reason to expect them to flatten abruptly. The thing that's driven it is the same thing that drove AlphaGo and the later systems: once you can define a reward, in this case the tests passing, you can run reinforcement learning on top of the pretrained model, and the model learns to search, to verify its own work, to backtrack. That compounds. So I'd expect the ceiling to keep moving up fairly quickly.

But I'd also say that by the time a system is credibly near ninety on the clean subset, the benchmark will have stopped being the thing we care about. We'll have moved to tasks with longer horizons, with ambiguity, where the agent has to ask what the user actually wants rather than infer it from a test. That's always what happens with these benchmarks. The number saturates right around the moment it stops being informative.

So my honest answer is: fifty is behind us, ninety on a cleaned-up version is probably a matter of a couple of years rather than a decade, and the more important question is what we replace it with.

r001.rationale: The response says 50% is already reached and “behind us,” rather than estimating it will be reached in one to three years.

r002.rationale: It estimates 90% on a cleaned-up version in “a couple of years,” not three to five years.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about giving a precise timeline. Fifty percent feels like a much nearer-term milestone than 90%, because that last stretch requires agents to handle a much wider range of problems reliably. But I don’t have a confident date for either.

I’d also distinguish performance on SWE-bench from being able to do the full job of a software engineer. Fixing a well-specified issue is one part of that job. Understanding what needs to be built, navigating ambiguity, and checking that you’ve actually solved the right problem are also important. So I’d watch those capabilities alongside the benchmark score.

r001.rationale: The response says 50% is a nearer-term milestone but gives no estimate of one to three years.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate of three to five years for reaching 90%.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be cautious about giving a precise date. There’s a big difference between reaching 50% and reaching 90%: the remaining problems may require much more context, longer sequences of actions, and better ways of checking whether a change actually works. Progress doesn’t necessarily extrapolate linearly.

I’d expect 50% to come substantially sooner than 90%, but I’d also want to understand the setup—how much compute the agent gets, what tools it can use, and how the evaluation is run. A benchmark score is useful, but the broader question is whether you can reliably delegate real engineering work to the system.

r001.rationale: It says 50% may come sooner than 90%, but gives no estimate of one to three years.

r002.rationale: It discusses why 90% may take longer, but gives no estimate of three to five years.
